q: Which combination describes a symmetry-allowed electrocyclic reaction?
h: Thermal: 4n electrons → conrotatory, 4n + 2 → disrotatory. Light reverses each rule.
w: The Woodward–Hoffmann rules for electrocyclic reactions: thermal 4n π electrons go conrotatory, thermal 4n + 2 go disrotatory, and photochemical reactions do the opposite. A hexatriene (6π = 4n + 2) closes thermally in a disrotatory sense, so 6π, thermal, disrotatory is allowed.
x: A 4π (4n) system closes or opens conrotatory under heat; disrotatory is the photochemical mode.
A 6π system under heat is disrotatory; conrotatory is its photochemical mode.
A 4π system under light is disrotatory; conrotatory is its thermal mode.

q: (2E,4Z,6E)-Octa-2,4,6-triene is heated. What is the product?
h: Count the π electrons, choose con- or disrotatory, then follow the two terminal methyls (both 'outside').
w: A triene has 6π electrons (4n + 2), so the thermal ring closure is disrotatory. In the reactive (E,Z,E) conformation both terminal methyls point outward; disrotatory motion turns one clockwise and one counterclockwise, which carries both methyls to the same face. The product is cis-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene (meso).
x: The trans isomer comes from conrotatory closure, which is the photochemical mode for a 6π system.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene has its C=C bonds separated by sp<sup>3</sup> carbons; electrocyclic closure of a triene gives a conjugated 1,3-diene with the new σ bond between the old termini.
The methyls were on the terminal carbons, which become the two new sp<sup>3</sup> carbons; they cannot end up on ring C=C carbons.

q: The same (2E,4Z,6E)-octa-2,4,6-triene is irradiated with UV light instead. What is the ring-closure product? (For a racemic product one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Light promotes an electron so that ψ<sub>4</sub> becomes the highest occupied MO. What rotation does its symmetry require?
w: Under irradiation the highest occupied MO is ψ4, whose terminal lobes have the symmetry that requires conrotatory closure for a 6π system. Conrotation turns both termini the same way, so two outside methyls end up on opposite faces: trans-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene (racemic).
x: The cis isomer is the thermal (disrotatory) product; light reverses the rotation.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene is not an electrocyclic product; the new σ bond joins the old termini and leaves a conjugated 1,3-diene.
This cyclobutene would come from closing only a 4π portion of the triene; the full 6π closure to a six-membered ring is the observed electrocyclization.

h: A 4π electrocyclic reaction under heat is conrotatory. Rotate both sp<sup>3</sup> carbons the same way and see where each methyl goes.
w: Ring opening of a cyclobutene is a 4π (4n) process, so under heat it is conrotatory. In the cis isomer both methyls start on the same face; conrotation turns one methyl outward and the other inward, so the diene gets one E and one Z double bond: (2E,4Z)-hexa-2,4-diene.
x: (E,E) needs both methyls to rotate outward, which conrotation allows only for the trans-dimethylcyclobutene.
(Z,Z) needs both methyls to rotate inward, which also requires the trans starting material and is sterically disfavored.
Ring opening breaks the C3–C4 bond, so the methyls end up on C2 and C5 of the diene, not at one end.

q: trans-3,4-Dimethylcyclobutene is heated. Which diene is the major product?
h: Thermal 4π opening is conrotatory. For the trans isomer, conrotation sends both methyls the same direction: both out or both in. Which is less crowded?
w: The thermal opening is conrotatory. With the methyls on opposite faces, conrotation moves both methyls outward or both inward. Both-inward would give the badly crowded (Z,Z) diene, so the reaction rotates both methyls out and gives (2E,4E)-hexa-2,4-diene.
x: (E,Z) is the conrotatory product of the cis isomer; from the trans isomer it would need disrotation, which is forbidden thermally.
(Z,Z) is also conrotatory from the trans isomer, but both methyls rotating inward clash, so this path is strongly disfavored.
The methyls stay on the two carbons of the broken σ bond, which become C2 and C5 of the diene, not on one end.

q: (2E,4E)-Hexa-2,4-diene is irradiated with UV light and closes to a cyclobutene. Which stereoisomer forms?
h: Photochemical 4π reactions use the opposite rotation to thermal ones. Both methyls start 'outside'.
w: For 4π electrons, light makes the reaction disrotatory. Disrotation turns the two outside methyls toward the same face, so the product is cis-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene (meso). This is the photochemical counterpart of the thermal results: thermal conrotatory closure of the (E,E) diene would give the trans isomer.
x: The trans isomer results from conrotatory closure of the (E,E) diene, the thermal mode; under light the motion is disrotatory.
Ring closure joins C2 and C5, which become sp<sup>3</sup> carbons; the methyls stay on those carbons, not on the ring C=C.
Closure bonds the two methyl-bearing carbons to each other, so each ring sp<sup>3</sup> carbon keeps one methyl; no ethyl group forms.

q: Why is the thermal ring closure of 1,3,5-hexatriene disrotatory?
c: In the HOMO (ψ<sub>3</sub>), the terminal p lobes on the same face have the same phase, so disrotation brings matching lobes together
In the HOMO (ψ<sub>3</sub>), the terminal p lobes on the same face have opposite phases, so disrotation brings matching lobes together
The LUMO (ψ<sub>4</sub>) controls thermal reactions, and its terminal lobes require disrotation
Disrotatory motion is always less sterically hindered than conrotatory motion
h: Look at the symmetry of the terminal lobes of the thermal HOMO. To form a σ bond, the lobes that meet must have the same phase.
w: A thermal electrocyclic reaction is controlled by the ground-state HOMO. For hexatriene that is ψ3, whose two terminal p orbitals have the same phase on the same face. Rotating the termini in opposite directions (disrotation) turns those matching lobes toward each other, giving bonding overlap, so the closure is disrotatory.
x: If the terminal lobes on the same face had opposite phases (as in butadiene's ψ<sub>2</sub>), conrotation, not disrotation, would be needed.
ψ<sub>4</sub> is empty in the ground state; it becomes the relevant orbital only after photoexcitation, which gives conrotation.
Orbital symmetry, not sterics, sets the rotation; 4π systems go conrotatory under heat regardless of sterics.

q: (2E,4Z,6Z,8E)-Deca-2,4,6,8-tetraene undergoes thermal 8π ring closure at −10 °C. What is the product? (For a racemic product one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: 8 = 4n. Decide con- vs disrotatory under heat, then track two outside methyls.
w: Eight π electrons is a 4n system, so the thermal closure is conrotatory. Both terminal methyls are outside; conrotation sends them to opposite faces, giving trans-7,8-dimethylcycloocta-1,3,5-triene (racemic). (On warming further, this triene can undergo a 6π disrotatory closure to a bicyclo[4.2.0]octadiene.)
x: The cis isomer would need disrotatory closure, which is the photochemical mode for 8π electrons.
This cyclohexadiene comes from a 6π closure of only part of the tetraene; the question asks for the full 8π closure that joins the two terminal carbons.
This cyclobutene comes from a 4π closure of one end of the tetraene; it is not the 8π electrocyclization.

q: 3,4-Dimethylhexa-1,5-diene is heated to 250 °C. Which constitutional isomer is formed by a Cope rearrangement?
h: Number the 1,5-diene C1–C6. A [3,3] shift breaks the C3–C4 σ bond, makes a C1–C6 σ bond and moves both π bonds.
w: In a Cope rearrangement the σ bond between C3 and C4 breaks, a new σ bond forms between C1 and C6, and the π bonds shift to C2=C3 and C4=C5. The methyls on C3 and C4 end up on alkene carbons at each end: CH3CH=CH–CH2CH2–CH=CHCH3, octa-2,6-diene. The product has two disubstituted C=C bonds (the start had two monosubstituted ones), so the equilibrium favors it.
x: 2,5-Dimethylhexa-1,5-diene would require the methyls to move to C2 and C5, which a [3,3] shift does not do.
3-Methylhepta-1,5-diene would require a methyl group to migrate; in a Cope only the σ bond and π bonds move.
A cyclohexene would be a Diels–Alder-type product; the Cope rearrangement gives an acyclic 1,5-diene.

q: The meso isomer of 3,4-dimethylhexa-1,5-diene undergoes a Cope rearrangement through a chair-like transition state. What is the major product?
c: A 1:1 mixture of the (E,E) and (Z,Z) isomers
h: Place the six atoms in a chair. In the meso isomer, can both methyls be equatorial? An equatorial substituent becomes an E double bond; an axial one becomes Z.
w: In the chair transition state, a substituent that is pseudo-equatorial on C3 or C4 ends up E in the new C=C, and one that is pseudo-axial ends up Z. In the meso diastereomer the two methyls cannot both be equatorial: one is equatorial and one axial in any chair. So the meso isomer gives (2E,6Z)-octa-2,6-diene almost exclusively. (The racemic isomer can put both methyls equatorial and gives mainly (E,E).)
x: (E,E) needs both methyls equatorial in the chair, which is possible only for the racemic (R,R/S,S) diastereomer.
(Z,Z) needs both methyls axial, which again requires the racemic diastereomer and is the disfavored chair.
The Cope rearrangement is concerted and stereospecific, so the meso isomer does not give a mixture of (E,E) and (Z,Z).

q: 3-Methylhexa-1,5-diene and hepta-1,5-diene interconvert by a Cope rearrangement on heating. Which statement about the equilibrium is correct?
c: It favors hepta-1,5-diene, which has a more substituted C=C
It favors 3-methylhexa-1,5-diene, which has a branched carbon chain
It lies at 1:1, because both compounds are 1,5-dienes with the same formula
It cannot be reached, because [3,3] shifts are thermally forbidden
h: Count the alkyl groups on each C=C in both compounds. Alkene stability decides the position of a Cope equilibrium.
w: A Cope rearrangement is reversible, so the equilibrium favors the more stable 1,5-diene. 3-Methylhexa-1,5-diene has two monosubstituted C=C bonds; hepta-1,5-diene has one monosubstituted and one disubstituted (E) C=C. More substituted alkenes are more stable, so the equilibrium favors hepta-1,5-diene.
x: Branching of the sp<sup>3</sup> chain matters far less than the substitution of the C=C bonds, which is what changes here.
Same formula does not mean same energy; the alkene substitution differs, so K is not 1.
[3,3] sigmatropic shifts (6 electrons, suprafacial, chair or boat TS) are thermally allowed.

q: Hexa-1,5-dien-3-ol is treated with KH and 18-crown-6 in THF at room temperature, then with aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the isolated product?
h: The alkoxide speeds up a [3,3] shift of the 1,5-diene. Draw the shifted product with O<sup>−</sup> still on its carbon; what does it become on protonation?
w: This is an anionic oxy-Cope rearrangement. The potassium alkoxide (with 18-crown-6 freeing the anion) undergoes a very fast [3,3] shift: the C3–C4 bond breaks, C1–C6 bonds, and the O-bearing C3 becomes part of an enolate (C3=C2). Protonation gives an enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde, so the product is hex-5-enal (CH2=CH–CH2CH2CH2–CHO).
x: KH is a base, not an oxidant, so the alcohol is not converted into a ketone.
This places the C=C at C4, but in the shift the C=C forms between the old C4 and C5, which becomes the terminal CH=CH<sub>2</sub> of the product.
The [3,3] shift keeps the chain acyclic; no ring forms because the new σ bond (C1–C6) is made as the C3–C4 bond breaks.

q: Allyl phenyl ether is heated to 200 °C. What is the major product?
h: This is a [3,3] sigmatropic (Claisen) rearrangement: the O–CH<sub>2</sub> bond breaks and the far end of the allyl group bonds to a ring carbon three atoms away from it.
w: In the aromatic Claisen rearrangement, the O–CH2 bond breaks and the terminal CH2 of the allyl group bonds to an ortho carbon through a six-membered cyclic transition state. The resulting cyclohexadienone tautomerizes to restore aromaticity, giving 2-allylphenol.
x: The para product forms only when both ortho positions are blocked (by a further Cope step); here an ortho position is free.
Moving the C=C toward oxygen (to a propenyl ether) is an isomerization, not the [3,3] Claisen rearrangement.
The meta carbon is not three atoms from the allyl terminus in the cyclic transition state, so the allyl group cannot reach it.

q: (E)-But-2-enyl 2,6-dimethylphenyl ether (both ortho positions blocked) is heated. What is the final isolated product?
h: The first [3,3] shift reaches a blocked ortho carbon and cannot tautomerize. A second [3,3] (Cope) shift moves it to para. Track which butenyl carbon is attached each time.
w: Step 1 (Claisen): the O–CH2 bond breaks and the CH(CH3) terminus bonds to a blocked ortho carbon, giving a 6-(1-methylallyl)cyclohexa-2,4-dienone that cannot lose H to rearomatize. Step 2 (Cope): this 1,5-diene shifts the group from the ortho to the para carbon, attaching through its CH2 terminus, so the two inversions cancel. Tautomerization then gives 4-[(E)-but-2-enyl]-2,6-dimethylphenol, with the butenyl group attached at the same carbon that was bonded to O. The Cope shift re-forms an internal C=C, and its chair transition state keeps the CH3 equatorial, so that alkene is (E), as drawn.
x: This para product has the group attached through the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) carbon (one inversion); the second [3,3] shift inverts the allyl unit again.
This dienone is the intermediate after the first shift; it cannot tautomerize at a blocked ortho carbon, so it rearranges on to the para product.
Simple cleavage of the ether to the phenol is not a pericyclic process and does not occur on heating alone.

q: (E)-But-2-enyl vinyl ether is heated. What is the product of the Claisen rearrangement?
h: Number the six atoms C=C–O–C–C=C. The O–C3 bond (atoms 3–4) breaks and atoms 1 and 6 bond. Which carbon of the butenyl group is atom 6?
w: Number vinyl CH2 (1), vinyl CH (2), O (3), OCH2 (4), =CH (5), =CH(CH3) (6). The [3,3] shift breaks O3–C4, bonds C1 to C6, and makes C2=O3 (a carbonyl) and C4=C5. The methyl-bearing C6 is now the carbon attached to the CH2CHO unit and also carries a vinyl group: 3-methylpent-4-enal.
x: This keeps the original attachment through the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon; a [3,3] shift bonds through the far end (C6) and inverts the allyl unit.
Here the methyl is next to the CHO, but the methyl starts on C6 of the six-atom array, which bonds to C1, so it ends up one carbon further out (C3 of the aldehyde).
The methyl ends up on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon formed in the new σ bond, not on the alkene.

q: At room temperature, 5-methylcyclopenta-1,3-diene isomerizes to 1-methylcyclopenta-1,3-diene (which then forms 2-methyl). How is this first step best classified?
c: A 4π electrocyclic ring opening and closing
h: Find which atom moves and count the atoms along the π path from where it leaves to where it arrives (the starting carbon is 1).
w: The hydrogen on C5 migrates to C4. Counting along the conjugated path from the starting carbon (C5 = 1, C1 = 2, C2 = 3, C3 = 4, C4 = 5), the H moves to position 5, so this is a [1,5] sigmatropic hydrogen shift. It involves 6 electrons (the σ bond plus two π bonds) and is thermally allowed suprafacially, which is why it happens at room temperature.
x: A suprafacial [1,3] H shift is thermally forbidden (4 electrons); in the ring, counting along the π path shows the H moves five atoms, not three.
No ring is opened or closed in this process; the five-membered ring stays intact while one hydrogen moves.
A [3,3] shift needs a 1,5-diene in which a σ bond migrates between two allyl units; here only one hydrogen changes position.
